title: Random variables as measurable functions
objectives: Define a random variable as a measurable function, and its distribution as a pushed-forward measure.

screens.title: Outcomes behind a value
screens.prose: Two fair dice give 36 equally likely outcomes. The random number $X$ is their sum, and each cell shows its value.
screens.question: Tap every outcome with $X = 7$.

hints.text: A cell is in the set when its sum is 7.
They run along one diagonal of the table.

feedback.correct: Six cells. This set of outcomes is the preimage $X^{-1}(\{7\})$, and its chance is $\tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac16$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the cells whose shown number is 7.

byKey.diag: You tapped the doubles. Their sums are 2, 4, 6 and so on.

explain.text: The cells with sum 7 are the preimage of the value 7, written $X^{-1}(\{7\})$. It holds 6 of 36 outcomes, so $P(X = 7) = \tfrac16$.

screens.title: At most 4
screens.prose: Now ask for every outcome with a sum of at most 4: the preimage of $(-\infty, 4]$.
screens.question: Tap every outcome with $X \le 4$.

hints.text: Include every sum from 2 to 4.
Sum 2 has one cell, sum 3 has two, and sum 4 has three.
That is 6 cells.

feedback.correct: Six cells, so $P(X \le 4) = \tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac16$. Call this value $F_X(4)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap every cell with sum 2, 3 or 4.

byKey.only4: You tapped only the sum of exactly 4. At most 4 includes 2 and 3 too.
byKey.lt4: You stopped at 3. A sum of exactly 4 is also at most 4.

explain.text: Sums 2, 3 and 4 have 1, 2 and 3 cells, so 6 cells in all. The chance $P(X \le 4) = \tfrac16$ is the value of the distribution function $F_X$ at 4.

screens.title: Random variables as functions
screens.prose: A **random variable** is a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\{X \le x\} \in \mathcal{F}$ for every $x$. Its **distribution** is the pushed-forward measure $P_X(B) = P(X^{-1}(B))$. Its **distribution function** is $F_X(x) = P(X \le x)$.
screens.question: Why must $\{X \le x\}$ be an event?

options.text: Otherwise $P(X \le x)$ has no value, as $P$ only measures events.
So that $X$ takes only finitely many values, as a die does.
options.why: You tied events to finite ranges. Random variables may take uncountably many values.

options.text: So that $X$ is continuous, with no jumps in its graph.
options.why: You tied events to continuity. A die roll is a random variable and is not continuous.

options.text: So that $F_X$ is increasing, like any distribution function.
options.why: Increasing comes from monotonicity of $P$. The condition is what makes $F_X$ defined at all.

hints.text: Ask which sets $P$ can measure.
$P$ is defined on $\mathcal{F}$ only.
$P(X \le x)$ is $P$ of the set $\{X \le x\}$.

feedback.correct: A chance needs an event. Measurability is exactly that requirement.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which sets $P$ is defined on.

explain.text: $F_X(x) = P(\{X \le x\})$ means something only when that set is in $\mathcal{F}$. So a random variable is a function whose sub-level sets are events.

screens.title: Measurable against less information
screens.prose: Suppose we see only the first die: $\mathcal{G} = \sigma(\text{first die})$, with the six rows as atoms. A function is $\mathcal{G}$-measurable when it is constant on every atom.
screens.question: Select all that apply. Which are $\mathcal{G}$-measurable?

options.text: The square of the first die
The sum of the two dice
options.why: You picked the sum. In row 3 it takes the values 4 to 9, so it is not constant on that atom.

options.text: The larger of the two dice
options.why: You picked the maximum. In row 3 it is 3 or more, so it is not constant on the atom.

hints.text: Check each function on one row.
In row 3 the first die is 3, so any function of it alone is fixed there.
The sum and the maximum change along the row.

feedback.correct: The three functions of the first die. Each is constant on every row.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each function along one row.

byKey.sum: The sum changes along a row.
byKey.max: The maximum changes along a row once the second die beats the first.

explain.text: A function of the first die alone is fixed along each row, so it is measurable for $\mathcal{G}$. The sum and the maximum depend on the second die as well. They need the full information.

screens.title: The distribution function of the sum
screens.prose: The chart draws $F_X$ for the sum. It jumps at each value, and each step starts with a closed dot at its left end.
screens.question: What is $F_X(7)$? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: $F_X(7)$ is the chance of a sum of at most 7.
Count cells with sums 2 to 7: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6.

feedback.correct: 0.5833. At 7 the step has already risen, because the closed dot sits at the left end.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the chances of the sums 2 to 7.

byKey.pmf: You gave $P(X = 7)$. $F_X(7)$ adds every sum up to 7.
byKey.lt: You gave $P(X < 7) = \tfrac{15}{36}$. $F_X(7)$ includes the sum of 7 itself.
byKey.next: You read the step after 7. $F_X(7)$ is the level at 7 itself.

explain.text: The sums 2 to 7 have $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21$ of the 36 cells, so $F_X(7) = \tfrac{21}{36} = \tfrac7{12}$. At a jump the value is the top of the step: the closed dot.

screens.title: Distribution functions are right-continuous
screens.prose: We prove $F(x + h) \to F(x)$ as $h \downarrow 0$ for $F = F_X$. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order, a reason in each line. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Fix $x$. The events $E_n = \{X \le x + \tfrac1n\}$ decrease as $n$ grows.
Their intersection is $\{X \le x\}$: an outcome with $X \le x + \tfrac1n$ for every $n$ has $X \le x$.
Probabilities are finite, so continuity from above gives $F(x + \tfrac1n) \to F(x)$.
$F$ never decreases, so $F(x + h) \to F(x)$ for every $h \downarrow 0$, not only $h = \tfrac1n$.
The events $\{X \le x - \tfrac1n\}$ decrease to $\{X \le x\}$.
lines.why: You used the wrong sets. Those events increase, and they approach $\{X < x\}$.
You used continuity from below. The events $E_n$ decrease, so the rule is continuity from above.

hints.text: Squeeze $x$ from the right with the events $\{X \le x + \tfrac1n\}$.
They shrink, and probabilities are finite, so continuity from above is allowed.
Order: shrinking events, their intersection, the limit, every $h$, the conclusion.

feedback.correct: Right. The step functions of the chart jump up at each value and meet the closed dot from the right.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Name the events and their intersection before you use a limit.

byKey.d1: You used the shrinking-from-the-left line. Those sets grow.
byKey.d2: You used the wrong continuity rule for shrinking sets.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: The events $\{X \le x + \tfrac1n\}$ shrink to $\{X \le x\}$, so continuity from above gives right-continuity. The same trick with $\{X \le x - \tfrac1n\}$ grows to $\{X < x\}$. By continuity from below, the left limit is $P(X < x)$.

screens.title: A loss with an atom
screens.prose: A portfolio loss $L$ is £0 with chance 0.9. Otherwise it is exponential with mean £10,000. The chart, in £000, shows the jump at 0: an atom of size 0.9, then a smooth rise.
screens.question: What is $F_L$ at £5,000? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Add the atom at 0 to the chance of a loss in $(0, 5{,}000]$.
The second part is $0.1 \times (1 - e^{-5000/10000})$.

feedback.correct: 0.9393: the atom 0.9 plus $0.1 \times 0.3935$ from the exponential part.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the atom to the chance from the smooth part.

byKey.atom: You gave $F_L(0)$. The smooth part adds more by £5,000.
byKey.tail: You gave only the smooth part. The atom of 0.9 is also at most £5,000.
byKey.exp: You gave $1 - e^{-0.5}$ without the weight 0.1 and the atom 0.9.

explain.text: $P(L \le 5{,}000) = P(L = 0) + P(0 < L \le 5{,}000) = 0.9 + 0.1(1 - e^{-0.5}) = 0.9393$. The chart jumps by 0.9 at 0 and then rises smoothly.

screens.title: Reading a jump
screens.prose: On the loss chart, $F_L(0) = 0.9$. A colleague reads this as "the chance the loss is below £0".
screens.question: What is $P(L < 0)$?

options.why: You read $F_L(0)$ as $P(L < 0)$. It is $P(L \le 0)$ and includes the atom at 0.

options.text: 0.1, what is left after the atom.
options.why: You gave the chance of a positive loss, $P(L > 0)$.
You split the jump. At a jump the value is the top of the step, not its middle.

hints.text: $P(L < 0)$ excludes the point 0.
The atom is at 0 itself, so it is not below 0.
$F_L(x) = 0$ for every $x < 0$, so $P(L < 0)$ is the left limit, 0.

feedback.correct: 0. $F_L(0) = 0.9$ is $P(L \le 0)$, and the two differ by the atom $P(L = 0) = 0.9$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $P(L < 0)$ leaves out the point 0.

byKey.b: The value at 0 counts the atom.
byKey.d: A jump has no middle value.

explain.text: $P(L < 0)$ is the limit of $F_L(x)$ as $x \uparrow 0$, which is 0. $P(L \le 0) = F_L(0) = 0.9$. The jump $F_L(0) - F_L(0^-) = 0.9$ is the chance of the single point.

screens.title: Pushing a measure forward
screens.prose: On a finite space the pushforward is a sum. Write `pushforward(probs, X)`. It takes `probs`, a dict from outcome to chance. It returns a dict from value to `Fraction`, the distribution of $X$. Then write `cdf(dist, x)`, which adds the chances of the values up to $x$.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

def pushforward(probs, X):

    ...

def cdf(dist, x):

    ...

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests with exact fractions. They cover two dice, three tosses, and the distribution function at and between the values.

hints.text: Loop over the outcomes and add each chance to the bucket of its value.
`dist[X(w)] += probs[w]`, starting each bucket at `Fraction(0)`.
`cdf` sums `p` over every value `v <= x`, so a value between steps gives the step below.

feedback.correct: Right. The preimage sums reproduce $\tfrac16$, $\tfrac{11}{36}$ and $\tfrac7{12}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add chances into one bucket per value, and keep `Fraction`s.

explain.text: The pushforward collects, for each value, the chances of the outcomes mapped to it. That is $P(X^{-1}(\{v\}))$. The distribution function adds those chances up to $x$.

screens.title: Value at risk by inverse sampling
screens.prose: A Monte Carlo engine draws $U$ uniform and sets $L = F^{-1}(U)$, where $F^{-1}(u) = \inf\{x : F(x) \ge u\}$. For the loss above this is £0 when $u \le 0.9$, and $-10{,}000 \ln\big(1 - \tfrac{u - 0.9}{0.1}\big)$ otherwise.
screens.question: What is the 95% value at risk, $F^{-1}(0.95)$, in £?

hints.text: Set $F(x) = 0.95$ and solve for $x$.

feedback.correct: £6,931.47. Draws with $u \le 0.9$ all give £0, because they land in the atom.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For $u > 0.9$ solve $F(x) = u$.

byKey.zero: You used the atom. $u = 0.95$ is above 0.9, so it lands in the smooth part.
byKey.mean: You used the mean loss. The 95% value solves $F(x) = 0.95$.

explain.text: The generalised inverse is the smallest $x$ with $F(x) \ge u$. At the atom it is £0 for every $u \le 0.9$, which is why plain inversion needs the infimum. For $u = 0.95$ it gives $10{,}000 \ln 2 = $ £6,931.47.

ideas: A random variable is a function with $\{X \le x\} \in \mathcal{F}$ for every $x$. Its distribution is the pushed-forward measure $P_X(B) = P(X^{-1}(B))$.
A function is measurable against a smaller sigma-algebra when it is constant on its atoms. The distribution function is right-continuous, with left limit $P(X < x)$.
At an atom the value $F(x) = P(X \le x)$ differs from $P(X < x)$ by the jump, so inverse sampling uses $\inf\{x : F(x) \ge u\}$.

formula.name: Distribution function
formula.note: Further reading: Williams, chapters 1 to 3, and Shreve II, chapter 1.

summary.trap: F(x) is P(X at most x), not P(X below x): the two differ at an atom.

quiz.prose: Let $U$ be uniform on $(0, 1)$ and $X = -\ln U$.
quiz.question: What is $P(X > 2)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $X > 2$ as an event about $U$.

byKey.two: You gave 0.2. The event is $U < e^{-2} = 0.1353$, because $-\ln U > 2$.
byKey.half: 0.5 is the chance that $X > \ln 2$, not $X > 2$. Undo the logarithm: $U < e^{-2}$.

explain.text: $-\ln U > 2$ means $U < e^{-2}$, and the uniform chance of that is its length, $e^{-2} = 0.1353$. So $X$ is exponential with rate 1.

options.why: You gave the value of $F$ at $x$. The left limit leaves out the atom.
You gave the size of the jump, $F(x) - F(x^-)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The left limit stops just short of $x$.

explain.text: The events $\{X \le x - \tfrac1n\}$ grow to $\{X < x\}$. Continuity from below gives $F(x^-) = P(X < x)$.

quiz.prose: Let $A \subseteq \Omega$ and let $\mathbf{1}_A$ be 1 on $A$ and 0 elsewhere.
quiz.question: When is $\mathbf{1}_A$ a random variable?

options.text: Always, since it takes only the values 0 and 1.
options.why: You looked only at the values. The sets $\{\mathbf{1}_A \le x\}$ include $A^c$, which must be an event.
You tied it to the size of $A$. An event of chance 0 still gives a random variable.

feedback.correct: $\{\mathbf{1}_A \le 0\} = A^c$, so $A$ must be an event.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the sets $\{\mathbf{1}_A \le x\}$.

explain.text: The sub-level sets are $\varnothing$, $A^c$ and $\Omega$. They are all events exactly when $A$ is. A constant is measurable for every $\mathcal{F}$.

quiz.prose: Two fair dice, with $X$ their sum.
quiz.question: What is $P(X \ge 11)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cells with sum 11 or 12.

byKey.one: You counted only the cell (6, 6). Sums of 11 and 12 give three cells.
byKey.two: You counted six cells. Only (5, 6), (6, 5) and (6, 6) have a sum of at least 11.

explain.text: Sum 11 has two cells and sum 12 has one, so $P(X \ge 11) = \tfrac{3}{36} = 0.0833$. Equivalently $1 - F_X(10) = 1 - \tfrac{33}{36}$.
